e90bf8500398a4f9: Open-weight models more than quadrupled their share of spending through Vercel's AI Gateway between June and September, when they processed more than seven in 10 tokens. "In August, open-weight models processed the majority of AI Gateway token volume for the first time," the biz said. "The money is now following. Open weight's share of spend has more than quadrupled over the last three months, from one in twenty gateway dollars in June to nearly one in four in September." AI Gateway, like OpenRouter, acts as an intermediary that allows customers to purchase tokens from different AI providers through a common interface. While it works with popular harnesses like Claude Code and Codex and provides access to proprietary and open-weight models, it doesn't see usage through other gateways or from customers who access AI models directly from vendors or through on-premises hosting. While gateway spending in September was about 13x higher than recorded in December 2025, the average price per token was about 47 percent lower, according to Vercel. At the same time, almost one in three teams changed their most-used AI provider in September, suggesting that market competition may be limiting vendor lock-in. The most popular model in September was TypeSafe AI's Jev. In just 14 days, it reached 35 percent of paid teams using Vercel's AI Gateway, the company said. Its popularity didn't generate much spending due to the model's architecture – usage accounted for only 1 percent of the month’s tokens and 0.15 percent of spending. US-based models from Anthropic and OpenAI still attract the largest portion of spending in September, with 11.03 percent going to Claude Opus 5.5, followed by GPT-6 Astra at 4.86 percent. But models from Chinese AI providers have become more popular. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ranked third in spending, at 4.19 percent. More than two-thirds of the September spending on Chinese models went to US providers serving those models, up from less than a tenth in December 2025, Vercel said. Moonshot AI, maker of Kimi, captured 3.6 percent of gateway tokens and 13.2 percent of spend in September; DeepSeek took 58 percent of tokens for just 6.6 percent of spend; and Z.ai, maker of GLM-5.3, took 7.2 percent of tokens and 4.5 percent of spend. So efforts to ban or limit open-weight models, something considered by the current US administration, would affect American businesses serving those models and their customers. Even if the US continues to dither on AI policy, trade barriers affecting AI models may alter market dynamics. China on Friday proposed adding 40 technology items to its export control list, 23 of them related to AI. The Associated Press notes that Moonshot’s Kimi K3 and Alibaba’s Qwen 3.8-Max are among the models that meet the parameter threshold set by Chinese authorities, though the official message did not identify affected models. "This introduces significant uncertainty for US businesses that host or rely on Chinese models," Chris McGuire, a senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, said in a social media post. "Particularly given that Chinese AI labs are moving toward licensing the use of open-source models to generate revenue, the Chinese government stating that it has the ability to curtail those licensing agreements at any time should make US businesses more hesitant to rely on those models going forward." McGuire said the US needs to adopt a comprehensive regulatory framework governing the use of US AI technology overseas and include Chinese AI models used or hosted in the United States in its domestic AI regulations.®

0a2b3ead2466f400: KUALA LUMPUR: Cable thieves continue to target transport infrastructure, with recent incidents involving the Kajang MRT Line and the New Klang Valley Expressway (NKVE) highlighting security concerns.
In the latest incident, thieves cut about 100m of cable between Phileo Damansara and Pusat Bandar Damansara stations early yesterday.
They abandoned it when auxiliary police and Prasarana personnel approached.
The thieves are believed to have rolled up the cables and left them aside for later collection.
Separately, PLUS Malaysia Bhd said its personnel and police had foiled a suspected cable theft attempt along the NKVE, leading to a suspect's arrest.
Photographs by PLUS showed what appeared to be cutting equipment, including a cordless power tool, a hacksaw, a hand saw and a toolbox, beside a concrete roadside barrier.
Another photograph showed damaged cables along a highway embankment, with sections exposed and out of place.
The incidents highlight the threat of cable theft to both railway and highway infrastructure.
MRT SERVICES DISRUPTED
The attempted theft on the Kajang MRT Line was detected about 5.30am after someone entered the track area between Phileo Damansara and Pusat Bandar Damansara stations.
Rapid KL said power to the affected section was temporarily cut in line with safety procedures.
The power cut allowed auxiliary police to inspect the area and search for suspects while protecting passengers, staff and railway facilities.
Power was restored at 6.32am after the checks were completed.
Rapid KL provided alternative services during the disruption so passengers could continue their journeys.
The company said cable theft could disrupt train services and endanger passengers and staff.
A police report was lodged at Brickfields police headquarters.
PLUS FOILS CABLE THEFT
PLUS said its personnel and police had arrested a suspect in an alleged cable theft attempt along the NKVE. The suspect was handed over to police at Sentul police headquarters
PLUS did not disclose when the operation took place or how much cable was involved.
Its photographs showed the scene and equipment suspected of being used in the theft.
PLUS said the theft or damage of highway facilities, including cables, safety barriers and road signs, could pose serious risks.
Such theft and damage could endanger motorists and affect highway safety systems.
The incidents have renewed concerns about cable theft syndicates targeting railway infrastructure using sophisticated methods.
Prasarana previously told the New Straits Times that cable thieves were exploiting hidden spaces in the concrete structures supporting elevated MRT tracks.
They have used openings in viaducts, nearby billboards and concealed spaces beneath elevated tracks to access the cables.
Prasarana had identified the area around Phileo Damansara as vulnerable because of its terrain and several entry points.
Prasarana has increased auxiliary police patrols and introduced canine units, better surveillance and additional physical barriers.
Prasarana previously said cable theft had cost it RM20.6 million over three years.
Cases rose from 42 in 2024 to 72 last year.
The operator said that 43 per cent of the 72 cable theft cases recorded last year involved access through concrete piers and viaduct structures.
Other access methods included breaches in perimeter fencing, hillside approaches and billboards.
The Kajang MRT Line is about 48km long and has 1,394 piers. The Putrajaya MRT Line is 68km long, with 1,265 piers.

bc3e46d458c39740: KUALA LUMPUR: A five-year-old girl was killed in a six-vehicle crash involving a BYD Seal along Jalan Kuching on Oct 10, in one of the week's most tragic incidents.
The girl was in the rear passenger seat of a Perodua Bezza driven by her 30-year-old father when the crash occurred as traffic moved slowly from the city centre towards Segambut.

Police said initial investigations found that the BYD Seal had rear-ended the Bezza, triggering a chain collision involving a Yamaha 135LC motorcycle and three other cars – a Nissan Almera, Toyota Alphard and Perodua Myvi.
The girl suffered severe head injuries and died en route to Hospital Kuala Lumpur. Her father injured his right hand, while the 33-year-old motorcyclist suffered head injuries.
The 24-year-old BYD Seal driver was admitted to a private hospital in Damansara for concussion treatment.
Here are the week's other major crime stories:
DRAMATIC POLICE CHASE IN WANGSA MAJU
Two men were arrested after a police chase from Bukit Antarabangsa to Setiawangsa on Oct 11. Videos of the pursuit and members of the public helping police went viral on social media.

Police pursued the suspects in an Isuzu D-Max pickup truck along Jalan Wangsa 5 in Bukit Antarabangsa towards the Middle Ring Road 2 before intercepting the vehicle at the junction of Jalan Jelatek and Jalan Taman Setiawangsa, near a petrol station.
A search of the vehicle uncovered a parang, a sickle, equipment believed to have been used to steal cables, including a manhole cover opener, and substances suspected to be drugs.
Videos showed the suspects trying to flee after their vehicle collided with other vehicles, while members of the public helped police apprehend them.
The case is being investigated under Section 186 of the Penal Code for obstructing a public servant, as well as provisions on offensive weapons and drug possession.
29 NABBED FOR PROMOTING UNLAWFUL ORGANISATIONS ONLINE
Police arrested 29 men, including a foreigner, in a nationwide operation targeting those suspected of promoting unlawful organisations on social media.

Codenamed Ops Mega TikTok 2026, the operation was conducted from Oct 10 to 12 by Bukit Aman's Criminal Investigation Department (CID), with the cooperation of the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission.

Bukit Aman CID director Datuk M. Kumar said the suspects, aged 18 to 49, were detained in coordinated operations involving 11 police contingents across Selangor, Johor, Pahang, Penang, Perak, Kuala Lumpur, Negri Sembilan, Kedah, Melaka, Sabah and Sarawak.
Police are also probing possible links between the suspects and other criminal activities, amid concerns over the use of social media to promote unlawful organisations.
14 ARRESTED IN CABLE THEFT CRACKDOWN
Police arrested 14 suspects linked to cable thefts in Selangor, Kedah, Melaka and Negri Sembilan.
The arrests came amid concerns over syndicates targeting telecommunications, railway and electrical infrastructure, with recent thefts disrupting essential services.
Crime experts have called for tougher action against scrap metal dealers suspected of buying stolen cables, warning that the illegal resale market fuels theft.
They said enforcement should target not only thieves but also the buyers and middlemen behind the trade.
5 MALAYSIANS HELD IN TOKYO OVER 5KG COCAINE HAUL
Five Malaysians have been arrested in Tokyo for smuggling 5kg of cocaine, prompting Malaysian border authorities to warn travellers against carrying luggage or parcels for others overseas.
Malaysian police will send an investigation team to Japan following the arrests.

Federal Narcotics Crime Investigation Department (NCID) director Datuk Hussein Omar Khan said the team would gather information about the arrests, including details of local and international drug syndicate networks.
He said Japanese authorities were tracing the cocaine's source and identifying those behind the smuggling attempt, including members of international drug trafficking networks.
POLICE PROBE ASSAULT, VANDALISM LINKED TO TASEK BERA OPERATION
Police are looking for a suspect who allegedly damaged a pickup truck and assaulted a man in Kampung Kuala Serting, Bera.
The suspect smashed a Toyota Hilux's side mirror, punched a man on the shoulder and fled on foot.
Police believe the incident was linked to a land enforcement operation by the Pahang State Enforcement Unit (UPNP) at the Tasek Bera Conservation Forest Reserve.
The UPNP and several other agencies are remeasuring the forest reserve to curb encroachment.
In recent weeks, several villagers have reportedly been arrested for obstructing enforcement personnel. Threats have also allegedly been made to stop the operation.
CUSTOMS OFFICER MURDERED, HUSBAND, ARRESTED
Police believe a marital dispute led to the death of a 35-year-old Customs officer, who was allegedly murdered by her husband in a public housing complex in Nilai on Thursday.
Initial checks indicated that the victim had been stabbed, with the weapon recovered at the scene.
The husband surrendered at the Bandar Baru Salak Tinggi police station in Sepang, Selangor.
The victim was a Customs officer who transferred to the Malaysia Border Control and Protection Agency (MCBA) service scheme on July 1.

dfddf2b0d286ab2a: KUALA LUMPUR: The deaths of young people featured prominently in court proceedings this week, from the murder of a 16-year-old girl by her classmate to a student killed in a crash on school grounds and a five-year-old girl killed in a six-vehicle pile-up.
In Batu Pahat, a Form 4 student was charged with murdering his classmate, Irene Sofiya Mohd Khairool Faisal, at their school in Yong Peng.

In Kota Baru, a teacher claimed trial to negligence charges over a crash that killed a Form 1 student and injured another. In Kuala Lumpur, a 24-year-old motorist denied causing five-year-old Asiah Ahmad Syahir's death through reckless driving.
Two other children's deaths also featured in court proceedings.
In Kota Kinabalu, the inquest into the death of 13-year-old Zara Qairina Mahathir concluded witness testimony after hearing from 83 witnesses.
In Johor Baru, the High Court detailed the abuse suffered by a three-year-old boy who died after being mistreated by a man entrusted with his care.

Elsewhere, a lorry driver claimed trial to driving under the influence of drugs in a 12-vehicle pile-up in Shah Alam, while former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak failed in his bid to suspend his 15-year jail sentence and RM11.4 billion fine in the 1Malaysia Development Bhd (1MDB) case.
Perikatan Nasional (PN) also obtained permission to challenge the Registrar of Societies' (RoS) decision to suspend its activities, but the High Court rejected its application for an interim stay.
Here are some of the week's major court cases and developments.
TEENAGER CHARGED WITH MURDERING CLASSMATE
A 16-year-old Form 4 student was charged with murdering his classmate, Irene Sofiya Mohd Khairool Faisal, at the Batu Pahat magistrate's court.
The accused nodded as magistrate Mustaqim Sukarno read out the charge under Section 302 of the Penal Code during closed-door proceedings.
He was accused of murdering Irene Sofiya at the hall of SMK Dato' Seth in Yong Peng between 2.30pm and 4pm on Oct 3.
Irene Sofiya's family members and members of the public gathered at the court complex to follow the proceedings.
She was found lying in the school hall with bloodstains on her body and bruises that appeared consistent with being beaten.
BYD SEAL DRIVER CHARGED OVER GIRL'S DEATH

The parents of five-year-old Asiah Ahmad Syahir sat in the last row of the public gallery at the Kuala Lumpur magistrate's court as the man accused of causing their daughter's death in a six-vehicle crash claimed trial.
Raeven Goh, 24, pleaded not guilty to three traffic offences, including causing Asiah's death through reckless driving along Jalan Kuching on Oct 10.
The bank sales manager also denied driving in a manner that endangered other road users and failing to stop and report the accident.
The court granted him bail of RM36,000 with one surety, ordered him to surrender his passport and suspended his driving licence pending disposal of the case.
TEACHER CHARGED OVER STUDENT'S DEATH AT SCHOOL

A 57-year-old teacher, Sakinah Ismail, pleaded not guilty at the Kota Baru magistrate's court to two charges involving negligence that caused a Form 1 student's death and injured another at SMK Tanjong Mas.
Sakinah was accused of driving a car that struck the two students within the school compound in April.
The case has drawn attention to student safety on school grounds.
LORRY DRIVER CLAIMS TRIAL OVER 12-VEHICLE PILE-UP
Lorry driver C. Agilan, 51, pleaded not guilty at the Shah Alam magistrate's court to driving under the influence of drugs in a 12-vehicle crash that injured four people.
He was accused of driving a 10-tonne lorry under the influence of methamphetamine and amphetamine along Persiaran Mokhtar Dahari in Alam Budiman on Oct 9.
The crash, involving 11 other vehicles at a traffic light junction, was captured on video and widely shared on social media.
Agilan also faced a separate charge of self-administering the drugs. His driving licence was suspended pending disposal of the case.
HIGH COURT DETAILS ABUSE OF THREE-YEAR-OLD BOY
The Johor Baru High Court detailed the abuse suffered by a three-year-old boy at the hands of a former e-hailing driver entrusted with his care.
Chan Wen Jie, 32, was sentenced to eight years and six months in prison for abusing the child, who died from his injuries.
In its grounds of judgment, the court described how the boy was forced to eat his own faeces from a diaper, an act it found degrading and unjustifiable.
CCTV footage also showed the child being hit, caned, forced to perform squats and made to stand for prolonged periods.
Chan pleaded guilty to an alternative charge of child abuse after an earlier murder charge was withdrawn. He was convicted and sentenced for abuse.
NAJIB FAILS TO SUSPEND 15-YEAR 1MDB JAIL SENTENCE AND FINE

The Special Corruption High Court dismissed former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak's application to stay the execution of his 15-year jail sentence and RM11.4 billion fine pending appeal in the 1Malaysia Development Bhd (1MDB) corruption and money laundering case.
Judge Noor Ruwena Md Nurdin ruled that Najib had failed to establish special circumstances warranting a stay of execution.
The sentence and fine remain in force unless a higher court orders otherwise.

However, Najib's lawyer, Tan Sri Muhammad Shafee Abdullah, said the decision would not affect his client's eligibility to serve the remainder of his sentence in the SRC International Sdn Bhd case under house arrest.

76fc1cdcd7e0a42b: GEORGE TOWN, Oct 17 — Graffiti in public toilet stalls and even schools filled with vulgar Hokkien phrases, crude drawings and declarations of love is largely frowned upon.
We don’t see so many of them anymore though and it’s a good thing.
But artist Sumidik is using his memory of this as a way to encourage the use of Hokkien – once widely spoken by Penangites of all races – again.
Sumidik’s solo exhibition even features a toilet stall complete with a toilet bowl with walls for visitors to scribble their Hokkien graffiti on.
“I want to use this exhibition as a fun way to shine a spotlight on Hokkien as I feel many in the younger generation cannot speak Hokkien now,” he said.
His exhibition is titled MaiKea which means “fear not” in Hokkien, a clever call-out to people to not be afraid to use Hokkien and to come visit the exhibition.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Sumidik wants to shine a spotlight on Hokkien through the ‘MaiKea’ exhibition. — Picture courtesy of Sumidik
The exhibition, after all, is Sumidik’s way of encouraging the use of Hokkien among the younger generation and to remind them of phrases used by the older generation.
He said Hokkien is a living language that evolved over the years and used to be spoken in public spaces from kopitiams to the markets.

Phrases such as kopi-o peng mai liao (black coffee without sugar), teh si juak (hot milk tea without sugar), wah, tjin kui! (That’s so expensive!) or khi si lang! (Stressing me out!) were often heard in kopitiams or in markets.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The paintings and Hokkien Calendar illustration series in the ‘MaiKea’ exhibition. — Picture courtesy of Sumidik
“So, I want to spotlight all these familiar Hokkien phrases and expressions by putting a fun wordplay on them through direct translation in my art,” he said.
The exhibition features 14 prints of his Hokkien Calendar Illustration series, three paintings and sculptures of his iconic TuKao.

TuKao is the shortened form of the common Hokkien phrase ah tu ah kao (pig and dog) which was used to describe the common person on the street who is rough around the edges, loud and maybe even a little bit vulgar.

Among his calendar series are common phrases such as buai ya (a Hokkien adaptation of the Malay word buaya) which is often used to describe a playboy and beneath it is chi ko pek which is a closely linked phrase meaning pervert or dirty old man.
“There are also three paintings and the main attraction is the toilet stall for visitors to scribble their own phrases,” Sumidik said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The toilet stall installation for visitors to scribble Hokkien phrases on. Sumidik got started with a few while the rest was filled by visitors. — Picture courtesy of AikBeng Chia
The exhibition, which opened on October 9, has already seen many visitors letting loose and scribbling various phrases on the three walls of the toilet stall including some vulgar ones.
“It’s very interesting, the visitors went all out to conteng on the walls... there were even Singaporeans spelling their own version of Hokkien phrases,” he said.
The exhibition at Masshaus, 147A, Lebuh Victoria in George Town, is open to the public from Friday to Sunday (12pm to 6pm) until October 31.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
The opening of ‘MaiKea’ by Sumidik at MassHaus. — Picture courtesy of MassHaus
80f9b7c626cc0f6c: MIRI, Oct 17 — Licensed crocodile hunters Team Eric Cat sells an estimated 200kg of crocodile meat a month at RM20 per kg, but their activities are driven more by their interest in catching crocodiles and desire to help the community rather than commercial returns.
Team leader Eric Chong Fook Shin, 41, said they sell their catch to restaurants and individual buyers here, with the price covering both meat and skin.
Proceeds are shared among team members, while sales depend on buyer demand.
“If there are buyers, we sell it. If there are no buyers, sometimes we give the meat to our friends.

“For us, it is not just about selling the meat. We are interested in catching crocodiles, and we also want to help when people make complaints about them,” he told The Borneo Post when contacted yesterday.
Chong said the team has so far not exported any crocodile products, as this requires separate licences and additional procedures.
“The ribs and tail are among the most popular parts for consumption, while demand for other parts is lower.”
He added that he keeps the skulls of the culled reptiles, while the feet and claws are given to friends who request them for ritual purposes.
According to Chong, his interest in crocodile catching began sometime in 2020 when he joined a group of friends on hunting trips.
The activity later developed into a more organised effort, leading to the establishment of Team Eric Cat in June 2025 following a fatal crocodile attack in Marudi in April that year.
The team, which began operations in June 2025, currently has 13 licensed members.
Working with the Sarawak Forestry Corporation (SFC), they carry out crocodile-catching operations in rivers where complaints have been received.
Their operations cover Miri, Marudi and parts of Baram, depending on locations identified and arrangements made with SFC.
Chong said the operations are important as local residents continue to rely on rivers for daily activities, putting them at risk when crocodiles are present.
“Crocodiles suspected of attacking people are of particular concern because they can pose further threats to other river users.”
Through its cooperation with SFC, the team estimates it has caught hundreds of crocodiles.
Chong said a crocodile-catching licence is valid for six months, with a quota of five crocodiles per licence period.
“Renewing the licence provides a further quota of five, while a separate licence, valid for one year, is required to sell crocodile meat.”
The team’s operating expenses are sponsored by Oren Mart, which covers fuel, meals, and other costs incurred during operations.
The team’s activities form part of wider crocodile management efforts in Sarawak.
In a report published by The Borneo Post on Aug 16, SFC Crocodile Management Section wildlife officer Dr Mohd Izwan Zulaini Abdul Gani said 70 crocodile-hunting licences had been issued statewide.

More than 100 crocodiles were caught by licensed hunters in the first half of 2026, with the figure exceeding 200 when crocodiles caught during SFC’s own management operations are included. — The Borneo Post
4423c9cc4a48f809: ADDIS ABABA, Oct 17 — Lying on a hospital bed, rolled-up blankets propping up the remains of her legs, 10-year-old double-amputee Iyerusalem is among scores of civilians wounded in northern Ethiopia after fighting erupted last month.

“I was in our compound with my older brother and our horse when we were hit. My brother and the horse died,” she told AFP from Ayder Comprehensive Specialised Hospital in Mekelle, capital of the northern Tigray state.

Fighting broke out between the rebel Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and federal forces on September 23. The Ethiopian army pushed back the assault and seized Mekelle without a fight this weekend after TPLF leaders and troops abandoned the city.
Many of the wounded live in remote villages hours from the hospital along difficult roads where there has been fighting and shelling.
“Right now, my amputated legs hurt badly,” said Iyerusalem, who comes from Qarsole village in Alamata district, south of Mekelle.
“If I get medical treatment and can walk again, I want to go back to school,” she said, as her father Hiluf watched anxiously.
In the same hospital lies 12-year-old Hana, her face torn apart by a blast that broke her leg, and killed her mother and brother.
“First I heard a loud explosion, and the whole house shook. I was scared and did not even know what had happened. I could not open my eyes or my mouth,” she said.
“The sound of the explosion keeps coming back in my head.”
In a nearby room were Betelhem, 10, who suffered a broken leg, and her sister Melet, 6, who was injured in the neck. Their pregnant mother was killed by heavy artillery.
“The bomb hit our house directly, all these people have died, but no one is being held responsible. There is no government,” said Haftom, the father of the family, a 39-year-old shopkeeper.
‘Doing our best’
The hospital’s emergency co-ordinator Birhanu Hailemariam said many patients had come from southern Tigray.
In recent days 34 people wounded by “heavy artillery, drones, gunfire and explosives have arrived at our hospital,” he said, 23 of them children. One person had died.
Staff lacked basic equipment and medicine, including anaesthesia, he said, “but we are doing our best to treat everyone.”
While he said the situation was not as bad as the 2020-22 Tigray war, which killed an estimated 600,000 according to the African Union, there was an atmosphere of fear permeating the hospital.
Whether it is the rebels or the government “both are hurting people,” said another doctor, who asked for anonymity.
“We do not know who carried out the bombardment. It is war,” said Iyerusalem’s father, Hiluf, avoiding blaming either the TPLF or the federal forces out of fear of reprisals.
As his daughter stared impassively ahead, Hiluf pleaded for aid and assistance to help her recovery.
“I do not want to fight with anyone,” he said. “Let there be peace for us.” — AFP
5e3a5038eb421dfd: ABUJA, Oct 17 — Nigerian models donned outfits of seemingly impossible amounts of fabric folded and moulded into massive silhouettes, or overlapping in shingled, feather-like patterns.

The colourful, detailed textiles evoked Carnival — both Nigeria’s own, in the southeastern city of Calabar, or that of Rio de Janeiro fame — but were in fact splashing down a runway in Abuja, better known for being the sleepy seat of government than for avant-garde couture.

Nigeria Fashion Week, which wrapped up last Sunday, decamped from Lagos this year, trading the mega-city of more than 20 million — the nation’s economic and artistic mecca — for the centrally planned administrative centre, which nonetheless has developed its own, smaller creative scene.
“Abuja is slow, slow in every way. People are very laid back,” Lexy Mojo-Eyes, the dapper organiser of the fashion week, who cut his teeth in Lagos, told AFP.
“We want to change the dynamics, we want to build Abuja as a fashion city.”
A slowly changing city

Nigeria officially moved its capital from thronging, crowded Lagos in 1991. But even in 2026, Abuja can still look half-built, its pockmarked downtown home to modern office buildings alongside empty lots and even farms that pre-date its founding.

It doesn’t have Lagos’s famous, and infamous, raucousness — but neither does it have a riposte to the Lagos film industry, known as Nollywood, or its major corporate headquarters and roster of Afrobeats stars.
As Abuja has slowly filled in over the years, it has shed some of its sterile feel, hosting a photography festival, an international film festival and a burgeoning literary scene.

Part of the reason the show moved to Abuja was to increase dialogue between industry and government, organisers said.

“Government has to be that enabling environment,” including by reforming tourism and intellectual property law, culture minister Hannatu Musa Musawa told AFP, wearing a metallic silver, pink and blue dress as she sat in the front row at a Friday runway show.
Libyan designer Rabia Ben Barka, whose models showed off similarly shimmering dresses, told AFP she found Abuja — on her first trip to Nigeria — “so clean” and organised.
“Anyone who comes by, they greet you with ‘Good morning,’” said Ben Barka, considered the doyen of Libyan fashion and who once counted Muammar Gaddafi’s wife among her clients.

Some of her boxy silhouettes evoked retro women’s shoulder pads — and then, down the runway, strutted a man in a metallic silver-and-black pinstripe suit, complete with heeled leather shoes: souped-up businesswear for a capital city shedding its stuffy image.
Cost of living
Abuja is also drawing longtime Lagos players, including Chinwe Ezenwa, a handbag designer who opened a second factory in the capital in 2021.
“It’s a bit of a sleepy town,” Ezenwa, the CEO of Le Look, told AFP. “But it’s picking up.”
Lagos, for its part, still retains its own, separate fashion week.
And whether Abuja can support the workers needed to run a creative sector — designers, fashion students and entrepreneurs — remains to be seen.

Many residents are already forced beyond the suburbs by brutal housing costs, and the government has come under fire for razing green areas, farms and “gardens” — cheap, open-air restaurants situated in parks — in favour of luxury development.

Nigeria Fashion Week, which wraps Sunday, decamped from Lagos this year, trading the mega-city of more than 20 million -- the nation's economic and artistic mecca -- for the centrally planned administrative centre, which nonetheless has developed its own, smaller creative scene. — AFP pic
Despite the change in venue, some things are universal in Nigeria, whose creaking grid is as infamous as Lagos traffic: as the models prepared backstage Friday, the power briefly cut out.
As the lights flickered back on, baptism in blackout over, one attendee quipped that the show was now, officially, “very authentic”. — AFP
8e7b27472731b94c: SÃO TOMÉ, Oct 17 — The plump, bright-green vanilla pods growing in tiny Sao Tome’s vast leafy plantations may well end up in some of Europe’s finest dining.
Although better known for its cocoa, the central African island off the Gulf of Guinea has revived its cultivation of vanilla, the world’s second most expensive spice, after saffron.
While his mother used to grow cocoa, Ifrasio de Barros Rompao has invested in the green pods that will turn yellowish on the thick, flat leaf vines once harvest time comes.
Spurred on by the promise of more profits, the farmer recently ventured into growing vanilla.
“Vanilla, in terms of money, for me, is essential,” de Barros Rompao said on his sloping forest plot in the heart of the island.
“I have a big family at home, and with this crop I manage to provide for our needs,” he added.
Once nicknamed the “Chocolate Islands”, the Portuguese-speaking archipelago was the world’s leading cocoa producer at the beginning of the 20th century.
The Vanilla planifolia orchid is believed to have been introduced in 1880 as an offering by French colony Gabon to the Portuguese governor at the time.
Its cultivation never took off, neglected in favour of intensive production of sugarcane and later cacao and coffee.
But the volatility of global cocoa prices and the ageing of the island’s plantations have left Sao Tome scrambling to diversify its economy.
And hopes are pinned on its niche vanilla cultivation.
Lengthy but lucrative
Only saffron commands higher prices than vanilla, which “adds an extra income for farmers”, Juliette Dohar, co-founder of L’Atelier Vanilha, said.
The project was set up seven years ago and focuses on supporting the development of high-quality vanilla production in Sao Tome.
With cocoa, producers can expect to earn small amounts spread across the year.
Vanilla brings in “much larger sums once or twice a year”, said Dohar.
Her organisation buys the spice from around 50 farmers to process locally before exporting it to European markets.
Producing the sweet-smelling spice is a lengthy process.
Vanilla can take up to three or four years to develop its first flowers.
At their facilities in Pema Pema on the outskirts of Sao Tome’s capital, the plant, once harvested, undergoes a long, artisanal preparation process.
First, the green vanilla is dried in the gardens in the sun.
“We’re in a very humid environment, so we need to remove part of the moisture from the pod fairly quickly,” Francesco Mai, the other founder of L’Atelier Vanilha, said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Co-founder of L'atelier Vanilha France's Juliette Dohar (second-left), 31, works with staff members in the workshop, in Sao Tome, capital of Sao Tome and Principe, on August 7, 2026. The plump, bright-green vanilla pods growing in tiny Sao Tome's vast leafy plantations may well end up in some of Europe's finest dining. On the island of Sao Tome, where the mild, warm climate favours the growth of vanilla vines, cultivating the tropical orchid -- which involves a demanding process of manual pollination -- remains a largely underdeveloped sector. — AFP pic
Afterwards comes several months of drying indoors, massaging the pods, scalding, fermentation and curing.
The vanilla then turns from green to dark brown and develops its characteristic aroma.

“At full production, we’re at around 300 kilos. These are very small volumes, but the goal is to achieve high quality and target a premium market of fine grocery shops and Michelin-starred restaurants in France, Switzerland and Belgium,” Dohar said.
‘Carries its landscape’
Madagascar and Indonesia dominate the global market, accounting for more than 80 percent of production with around 3,000 tonnes between them.

On the island of Sao Tome, where the mild, warm climate favours the growth of vanilla vines, cultivating the tropical orchid — which involves a demanding process of manual pollination — remains a largely underdeveloped sector.
But more than 5,000 kilometres (3,000 miles) away, the vanilla of the “Chocolate Islands” is appreciated for its aromatic qualities.
“There are notes of cocoa nibs in the base notes,” said Mathilde Roellinger, managing director of Epices Roellinger, a renowned, Michelin-starred name in French gastronomy.
“There’s a real floral elegance with violet notes,” she said, from the family restaurant in Cancale Bay in northwestern France.

“Then at the heart of the vanilla you almost get hints of small red berries. It’s extremely rich in the diversity of its aromatic profile,” she added, breaking off to inhale the scent of a newly arrived pod from the island.
Its flavours give a tiny taste of the far-away archipelago of 210,000 people which gained independence in 1975.
“For me, every spice carries the landscape it comes from,” Roellinger said.
“And Sao Tome is a paradise island. There is a bit of that mystery and beauty in the vanilla bean.” — AFP
f5f1ee3ecb26174a: As analyses of Budget 2027 continue to unfold, attention has naturally shifted from the headlines toward detailed ministry allocations and how they translate into actual support for the domestic economy.

Among the wide-ranging fiscal announcements, a range of comprehensive policies dedicated to micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) stand out as both structurally necessary and politically astute.
Stewarded by Steven Sim, the entrepreneur and cooperatives development ministry have all the hallmarks of election-winning policies ahead of GE16.

The Madani government has designated 2027 as the Year of Malaysian MSMEs and rolled out a package that addresses longstanding business bottlenecks through its structured ABCD framework focused on productivity shift (Anjakan Produktiviti), simplified bureaucracy (Birokrasi Dipermudah), capital access (Capaian Modal) and market accessibility (Daya Akses Pasaran).

MSMEs are often cited as the backbone of the economy given that they make up 97.4% of all businesses in Malaysia, with micro enterprises taking up 77.4%, small firms 21.4% and medium-size firms 1.1%. They employ 8.1 million people, giving them a 48.7% share of the total workforce.
In 2025 MSME-driven GDP outpaced national GDP growth. With value-added it grew by 5.7%, exceeding the overall national GDP growth rate of 5.2%. MSMEs accounted for 39.7% of Malaysia’s total GDP.
Services and manufacturing have a combined share of 84.5% of MSME-generated GDP, with agriculture (8.4%), construction (5.3%) and mining and quarrying (0.5%) making up the balance.
MSME exports expanded by 10.5% to RM214.5 billion, driven by manufacturing exports which rose 8.8% and services exports that went up 14.0%, accounting for 14.7% of Malaysia’s total exports.
MSME labour productivity rose by 4.1% led by strong gains in construction which went up 10.8% and manufacturing rising 4.8%.

Rather than rely on broad, sweeping gestures, Budget 2027 provides calibrated relief and structural support targeting the pain points most frequently cited by business owners including operational cost drivers, raw materials, labour, transportation, logistics and utilities.

To address financing and liquidity, loan facilities and financing guarantees for businesses have reached a historic high of RM57 billion, up from RM50 billion in 2026. This includes substantial micro-financing allocations through institutions like Amanah Ikhtiar Malaysia, Tekun Nasional and Bank Simpanan Nasional.
The corporate income tax rate for MSMEs has been reduced by up to two percentage points, providing help for cost management and direct savings for approximately 300,000 enterprises.

Cutting operational red tape with practical measures, such as a 50% rental discount throughout 2027 for small traders renting DBKL premises, streamlined direct-appointment procurement procedures, and full stamp duty exemptions for new business accounts will be a real help and demonstrates an understanding of realities on the ground.

By prioritising practical problem-solving over rigid compliance, Sim has helped position the ministry to deliver meaningful support, such as RM30 million earmarked for AI and automation adoption, without alienating the business community.

When evaluated alongside the broader macroeconomic national budget, these interventions clearly serve a dual purpose. By addressing cost-of-living concerns, supporting local contractors through expanded Bumiputera procurement quotas and easing compliance burdens, the government has crafted a politically compelling narrative of economic stewardship.
It is these types of fine print that are often overlooked but they show that Budget 2027 balances fiscal ambition with electoral appeal.
If implemented effectively across agencies, these policies may well secure the vital grassroots backing the administration seeks as it heads toward the next election.

e8ac1a3c6a97f388: Peruntukan RM935 juta bagi memperkasa sektor pelancongan dan budaya mencerminkan keyakinan terhadap peranan industri ini sebagai pemacu ekonomi negara.

Seiring pelanjutan kempen Tahun Melawat Malaysia 2026 hingga tahun depan, peruntukan itu merangkumi promosi, penganjuran acara, penambahbaikan kemudahan serta sokongan kepada seni, budaya dan warisan.
Namun, pada pandangan saya, ukuran kejayaannya bukan terletak pada jumlah yang disediakan, tetapi sejauh mana pelaksanaannya memperbaiki pengalaman pelancong dan mengukuhkan ekonomi setempat.
Promosi perlu seiring kemudahan

Geran galakan untuk mempromosikan destinasi dan menganjurkan acara pelancongan boleh memperluas pilihan pengalaman serta menarik segmen pasaran berbeza. Namun, destinasi yang dipromosikan juga perlu bersedia menerima pelawat.

Justeru, perhatian terhadap penambahbaikan kemudahan, termasuk jeti dan tapak warisan yang berpotensi mendapat pengiktirafan Unesco seperti Lembah Danum, Lembah Bujang dan Taman Negara Pahang, adalah penting.
Tarikan yang hebat tidak memadai jika kebersihan, keselamatan, papan tanda dan kemudahan asas masih lemah. Semua ini membentuk pengalaman pelancong, bukannya perkara sampingan.
Begitu juga dengan peluasan pembayaran kod QR ke 15 lokasi pelancongan, termasuk pulau peranginan.
Langkah ini boleh memudahkan urus niaga di kawasan yang kekurangan mesin pengeluaran wang automatik (ATM), sekali gus mengurangkan risiko peniaga kecil kehilangan jualan akibat kekangan pembayaran.
Akses lebih mudah, perbelanjaan lebih bermakna
Penyediaan Geran Sepadan Penerbangan Antarabangsa dan Charter untuk merintis laluan terus baharu dari China, India, Asia Tengah dan Eropah pula menangani keperluan asas pelancongan, iaitu akses.
Destinasi sukar berkembang jika perjalanan untuk sampai ke sana terlalu panjang, mahal atau rumit.
Peluasan skop geran kepada kapal persiaran, feri dan bas persiaran turut membuka ruang untuk menjangkau pasaran yang kurang dimanfaatkan.
Pendekatan ini mengambil kira perbezaan pola perjalanan pelawat serantau dan pelancong kapal persiaran, tanpa bergantung pada penerbangan semata-mata.
Bagaimanapun, pembukaan lebih banyak laluan perlu disusuli usaha menggalakkan pelancong tinggal lebih lama dan berbelanja.
Kenaikan had pembelian barangan bebas cukai di Langkawi dan Labuan kepada RM10,000, tertakluk kepada penginapan minimum 48 jam, boleh menyokong matlamat ini.
Usaha memberi lebih banyak pengecualian duti kepada produk buatan Langkawi pula wajar dimanfaatkan untuk memperkukuh perusahaan tempatan.
Peningkatan perbelanjaan pelancong hanya memberi kesan terhad kepada komuniti jika sebahagian besar nilainya tidak kekal dalam ekonomi setempat.
Sokongan kepada pengusaha kraf tangan, tenunan dan batik juga perlu disertai pemasaran yang mengetengahkan cerita, identiti dan nilai budaya produk mereka.
Produk ini seharusnya menjadi sebahagian daripada pengalaman pelancongan, bukan sekadar cenderamata.
Acara besar mesti sesuai dengan kapasiti destinasi

Rebat kepada penganjur acara besar antarabangsa di lokasi yang mampu menampung sekurang-kurangnya 10,000 penonton berpotensi merangsang permintaan terhadap hotel, makanan, pengangkutan dan aktiviti bandar.

Namun, penganjuran mesti mengambil kira kemampuan destinasi menampung lonjakan pelawat. Tanpa perancangan yang baik, acara sedemikian boleh mengundang kesesakan, kenaikan harga melampau dan pengalaman yang mengecewakan.
Pelanjutan galakan cukai bagi lawatan insentif, persidangan dan pameran perdagangan antarabangsa sehingga tahun taksiran 2030 pula menyokong segmen acara perniagaan.

Segmen ini mempunyai corak perbelanjaan yang berbeza daripada pelancongan riadah. Penganjurannya perlu dihubungkan dengan produk tempatan supaya manfaat ekonomi tidak terhad kepada pusat konvensyen dan hotel.
Nilai hasil pelaksanaan
Kesemua langkah ini memerlukan penyelarasan antara agensi, destinasi dan penggiat industri. Tanpanya, pelaksanaan berisiko bergerak secara berasingan dan mengehadkan keberkesanan keseluruhan pakej.
Penilaian pula tidak boleh sekadar menghitung jumlah program atau peruntukan yang dibelanjakan. Ia perlu berasaskan hasil yang dapat diukur.
Antaranya ialah kelangsungan laluan baharu selepas insentif tamat, tempoh penginapan dan peningkatan perbelanjaan pelancong di luar destinasi utama.
Pertambahan pelanggan bagi pengusaha kecil serta kepuasan pelawat terhadap kemudahan yang dinaik taraf juga perlu diambil kira.

Tahun Melawat Malaysia seharusnya meninggalkan kesan yang melangkaui tempoh kempen: destinasi yang lebih berdaya saing, perusahaan tempatan yang lebih kukuh dan pengalaman yang mendorong pelancong kembali.

4918aa4e9cfbe7d9: KAJANG: For more than a century, the Tamilian Physical Cultural Association (TPCA) has helped shape athletes, stage sporting contests and bring communities together.
Now, more than four decades after losing the stadium it once called home, members are hoping to write a new chapter by building a permanent clubhouse at TPCA’s grounds in Saujana Impian here.

The association is aiming to raise RM600,000 through a fundraising dinner at Fui Chuai Restaurant in Sungai Chua on Dec 12. Together with RM1.5 million already in its coffers, the money would give TPCA the RM2.1 million it needs to begin the redevelopment.
Organising committee secretary Vivehananthan Vairakkannu said the response from members, supporters and the wider public has so far been encouraging.

“God willing, we will be able to achieve our targeted budget to make the redevelopment a reality within a year, for the benefit of the community and public in this region - especially the youth,” he said.
The project is about more than finally having a proper building - it is also about reviving an organisation that once produced a steady stream of state and national athletes across several sports.

“We wish to revive the glory days of TPCA, which helped contribute a regular supply of local and national athletes in various sports at the SEA Games, Asian Games, Olympics and world championships," Vivehananthan said.
“Our aim is to continue unearthing and nurturing talent for the country, without burdening the government.”

In 2000, TPCA purchased five acres (2.02ha) of land in Kajang, close to a golf club, and has since established sporting activities there. It hopes eventually to acquire an adjoining two acres (0.81ha), estimated at RM4 million, to accommodate a multipurpose hall.
For now, however, its facilities remain modest: the club operates from a makeshift tent while hosting activities such as pickleball, netball, football, hockey and cricket.
A permanent clubhouse would provide changing rooms, food and beverage outlets, a fitness centre and recreational facilities, among other amenities, Vivehananthan explained.
“We need a proper clubhouse,” he stressed, adding that the larger ambition is to create a place where young athletes can train, families can gather, and TPCA’s cultural traditions can continue.
That ambition draws heavily on a past that stretches back to 1914, decades before Malaya achieved independence.

The association eventually built what Vivehananthan describes as one of the country’s earliest privately owned stadiums. Constructed between 1953 and 1955 on swampy land beside Kuala Lumpur Hospital on Jalan Raja Muda Abdul Aziz, the 7,000-capacity TPCA Stadium cost RM85,000.
For members of that generation, it became much more than a sporting venue. “TPCA stood as a cornerstone of its community, athletic distinction and cultural pride,” Vivehananthan noted.
But in 1982, the association was required to vacate the site following a government acquisition, for which it received RM1.36 million. The former TPCA Stadium subsequently became Stadium Raja Muda.
Losing that home left a wound that members have carried for decades - which is why the Kajang redevelopment carries such significance.
“We stand at a pivotal milestone: financing and constructing our new TPCA clubhouse to serve future generations,” Vivehananthan added.
“This project reflects a long-awaited homecoming. This is more than bricks and mortar; it is an investment in continuity and excellence in sports and youth talent.”

He said TPCA hopes the new facilities will provide infrastructure, equipment and mentorship for emerging athletes, while also creating room for arts, music, vernacular-language classes, festive celebrations and the preservation of its own history.
Retired Royal Malaysian Air Force warrant officer Edward Victor remembers TPCA’s contribution to Malaysian sport being recognised at the highest levels.

During the association’s 50th anniversary in 1964, he recalled, then Selangor ruler Sultan Salahuddin Abdul Aziz Shah and Malaysia’s first prime minister Tunku Abdul Rahman both paid tribute to its achievements.
Victor said Tunku singled out TPCA’s contribution to football, crediting the association with nurturing numerous state and national players and helping grow the sport’s popularity.
The stadium itself hosted many notable matches, including the 1956 Malaya Cup final between Selangor and Singapore. It would later stage matches during the 1975 Hockey World Cup in Kuala Lumpur.
Victor also highlighted another part of TPCA’s legacy: its decision to open membership to people of all races as early as 1923.
He said that commitment reflected a belief that sport should have no barriers of race or creed - a principle TPCA continues to uphold in its teams today.
For members such as Victor, that history is precisely why the present fundraising effort matters.
He hopes the public will help create not merely another building, but a home where TPCA can continue producing athletes, preserving its heritage and bringing people together for decades to come.
After more than a century of adapting, rebuilding and carrying on, TPCA is now hoping its next generation will finally have a roof of its own under which to do the same.
23dcf4236d1c6c01: RABAT: Morocco's King Mohammed VI formally appointed on Friday the members of his country's new government, led for the first time in its history by a woman prime minister, Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri.

Her centre-right Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) came out on top in September elections, and has entered into a coalition with the right-wing Istiqlal party and two smaller left-wing parties. Together they hold 210 of the parliament's 395 seats.
Thirteen out of 31 ministers from the previous government were retained in the incoming cabinet, including Nasser Bourita as foreign affairs minister and Abdelouafi Laftit as interior minister.
PAM newcomer Fouzi Lekjaa -- a budget minister in the outgoing government better known as the head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation -- has been promoted to economy minister.
The new government also includes seven women, counting the prime minister, as did the previous one.
Following her royal audience on Friday, Mansouri touted an "ambitious government programme that can meet citizens' expectations".
September's vote, which saw the lowest turnout in nearly 20 years, was marked by concerns about the cost of living, employment and inequality.
The incoming government will have to address those concerns while also preparing for the 2030 World Cup, which will be co-hosted with Spain and Portugal.

f3c02b63302f9678: WASHINGTON: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia was pushed out Friday after less than a week in the high-profile job, following a series of blunders that added to distractions for her embattled boss President Donald Trump.
"Can confirm," a White House official told AFP, after Fox News reported that Zacharia, 41, was "transitioning out."

The writing was on the wall earlier when Trump made clear he was ready to see his newly minted spokeswoman go amid criticism that she had pretended to be a lawyer and over her one, much-mocked press briefing.
"I said, 'Katie, is this for you?'" Trump told reporters. "I said, 'Katie, you don't have to do this'... I said to her, 'Honestly if I were you I'd reconsider.'"

Zacharia only began her job five days ago, taking over from the combative Karoline Leavitt, who helped Trump reshape White House coverage by bringing in more friendly outlets and fiercely attacking critical media.
Zacharia had got off to a rocky start with her debut press room briefing Tuesday morning.
It lasted less than 15 minutes, beginning with a remarkably slow reading out of what she said were Trump's many accomplishments – then taking just three questions from journalists.
She then was plunged into controversy when it emerged that her previous claims to be a lawyer were not true.

The kerfuffle is a distraction for 80-year-old Trump as he flies around the country trying to boost Republican candidates ahead of the November 3 congressional midterm elections, with polls predicting a drubbing.
The Republican leader himself also faces ever-lower polls as Americans sour over the war against Iran, inflation and perceptions of corruption.
NOT A REAL LAWYER
Zacharia had described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and on social media, and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit.
While she does have a law degree from a California university, she acknowledged Thursday she had failed the bar exam, a prerequisite for practicing law in the United States.
She embarked on a series of damage-control interviews on Trump-friendly outlets, but they did no good.
In one of them, Fox News' Sean Hannity, a close Trump ally, appeared dismissive of Zacharia.
He asked the press secretary if she ever retook the bar exam. She replied: "I did not."
"It was never my intent to go into the practice of law," she said.

In another interview Thursday with pro-Trump outlet Real America's Voice, Zacharia said she had registered to take the bar exam but was "distracted and overwhelmed" by plans to move to China with her husband.
Zacharia said "many people in the field" had assured her that she could "label myself a lawyer," given her law degree.
CHINA'S TOILETS

"Fox and Friends," which often conducts friendly interviews with Trump administration officials, was unusually direct Friday when a host asked Zacharia if she still had the confidence of the president.
"I hope to be able to build the trust and confidence of everyone around me," she said, sidestepping the question.
Zacharia further stirred controversy on Thursday when she disparaged China, whose leader Xi Jinping was recently Trump's guest in a pomp-filled Washington visit.
The press secretary recalled the perception in 2016 was that China would soon overtake the United States.

"I remember this very distinctly, having just come from China, thinking, 'How is China the next country on the horizon? They don't even have proper toilets,'" she told right-wing influencer Jack Posobiec in an interview.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning responded Friday that Zacharia should "visit China more often."

384589f08d293c79: RAMALLAH: Israeli settlers on Friday attacked an American photojournalist working for The Washington Post while she was covering violence against Palestinian olive farmers in the occupied West Bank.
Heidi Levine, a veteran photographer, was taken to hospital in Ramallah following the attack, with AFP photos showing her lying on a gurney with injuries to her leg and hand.

The office of prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, days ahead of elections in which he is seeking settlers' support, insisted the circumstances behind the incident were unclear, in contrast with the full-throated condemnation offered by his chief rival.
The attack comes 10 days after settlers beat an AFP photographer covering the West Bank olive harvest, Jaafar Ashtiyeh, leaving him also requiring hospital treatment.

Speaking to journalists from her hospital bed, Levine said that "more than 50" masked settlers holding sticks suddenly attacked her while she was working near the Palestinian villages of Abu Falah and Turmus Ayya in the central West Bank.
"All of a sudden they jumped me and I luckily had my helmet and flak jacket on and I... kept my face to the ground to try to protect my face," she said.
"They just kept kicking me and kicking me," she added.
After receiving initial care in Ramallah, Levine was transferred to Israel's Beilinson Hospital in Petah Tikva, where doctors found she had suffered four broken vertebrae and would need surgery.
The Washington Post said Levine had been wearing a flak jacket clearly marked "Press".

"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," Matt Murray, the paper's executive editor, said in a statement.
'No mercy'
Netanyahu's office said Levine had been "allegedly assaulted", adding that the circumstances were "unclear and are under investigation".

"Those responsible will be held accountable," it said in an X post, giving a version of events in which "some 200 Arabs and far-left activists confronted approximately 40 Israeli youths", with both sides throwing objects at the other.
Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main rival in the upcoming polls, blamed Friday's "unacceptable" attack on a "handful of rioters" whose actions, he said, "stain an entire nation".
A US state department official said it condemned "criminal violence by any party in the West Bank" and called for "legal accountability for those responsible".
The official added the department had "reached out to the Washington Post to offer consular assistance".

AFP did not witness the moment of the attack, but one of the agency's journalists in the area saw Palestinian medics tending to someone on the ground and Israeli soldiers pushing away journalists trying to approach.
The Israeli military said troops and border police forces were deployed to the area "following a report of a violent confrontation".
"A female journalist had been injured during the confrontation," it said, adding the circumstances would be examined.
"Attacks and violence against innocent civilians are grave and unacceptable acts," the military said.
The Israeli police said it had opened an investigation into incidents in Abu Falah and Turmus Ayya.
"We were on our land, picking olives, and suddenly the settlers came down on us and started hitting us, throwing stones," said Mukhlis Zuhdi, a farmer from Abu Falah.
"There was even a foreign journalist whom they beat. These people have no mercy or compassion in their hearts," he told AFP.
'Brazen violence'
The Foreign Press Association, which represents international media in Israel and the Palestinian territories, said the settlers stole Levine's passport, phone, wallet and equipment.
"This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank," it said.
Reporters Without Borders said it strongly condemned the attack and called on Israeli authorities to "put an end to this impunity and prosecute the perpetrators of this heinous assault".

"This brazen violence... is evidence of the impunity with which extremist Jewish settlers operate, often under the protection of Israeli armed forces," added the advocacy group, known by its French initials RSF.
Violence has flared in recent months in the West Bank, with near-daily attacks, thefts or vandalism by Israeli settlers against Palestinians.

Excluding east Jerusalem, around three million Palestinians live in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, alongside more than 500,000 Israelis residing in settlements considered illegal under international law.
7581c2e48fb95aa1: BANGKOK: British finance minister John Healey said expanding Heathrow Airport would help drive growth, in a show of support for the project after his boss, prime minister Andy Burnham, refused to back plans for a new runway.

Adding an extra runway at the busiest airport in Europe is an issue that has divided British politicians for decades. Under Burnham's predecessor, Keir Starmer, the government sought to settle the matter in 2025 by saying it should go ahead.
Healey told reporters at the International Monetary Fund's annual meeting in Bangkok that the project was in line with the government's central aim of strengthening the economy.
"The case for a third runway at Heathrow has always been a case for growth," he said on Friday.
Three weeks ago, Burnham declined to support it and said the decision was a matter for people who live near the airport.

Many businesses, airlines and investors have said the airport should expand but some local residents have objected to the noise from more planes, while the UK's climate targets could be at risk from adding thousands more flights.

Heathrow faces a lengthy planning process before any potential construction can begin and the airport said in September that a third runway may not open until 2039, four years later than forecast in an initial plan.
b8005d4d420af893: WASHINGTON: The US budget deficit grew to almost US$2 trillion over the past year, government data showed Friday, reaching its highest level since 2021 despite president Donald Trump's promises to cut public spending.
The expansion comes amid growing worries over the massive US$40.3 trillion US debt load and rising inflation, as the cost of borrowing climbs.
Refunds of Trump's tariffs after they were overturned have further fuelled the budget gap.
The federal deficit, which occurs when government spending exceeds its revenues, rose to US$1.99 trillion in fiscal year 2026, the treasury department said.
This marked a 12% increase from the prior year, when the shortfall came in at US$1.78 trillion.
A key driver of expenditures was the rising interest paid on public debt, which jumped US$144 billion to a record US$1.36 trillion.
Interest costs on around US$32 trillion in publicly held US debt have been ballooning in recent years, and climbing bond yields have sparked further concerns.

Treasury bond yields, which influence interest rates for mortgages and auto loans, have jumped this year, with steeper borrowing costs adding to pressures that US voters face ahead of November's midterm elections.
Meanwhile, an expected influx of revenue from Trump's sweeping tariffs have failed to fully materialise during his second term.
The Supreme Court struck down his global duties in February, triggering a wave of refunds.
Treasury data released Friday reflected US$145 billion in customs refunds over the year -- primarily due to tariffs -- erasing significant gains from Trump's duties.
Overall, government revenues climbed by 3% to US$5.40 trillion in the latest fiscal year, which ended Sept 30.
But spending was much higher, rising by 6% to US$7.40 trillion.
War risks
The deficit will likely be similar for the next year, said Nancy Vanden Houten of Oxford Economics.
But she warned "the risk may be for a larger budget gap if the war with Iran persists well into the fiscal year."
The Trump administration has pledged to cut deficits and government spending since he returned to the White House last year.

Besides slashing the federal workforce and foreign aid, the Republican-controlled Congress pushed through cuts to the Medicaid health insurance scheme and moved to shrink the federal food assistance program too.
But they also extended expiring tax cuts and provided fresh funding for Trump's migrant deportation drive.
The latest data released Friday showed that upticks in tax collection from individuals and customs revenues were offset by higher refunds and lower corporate tax collection.
Among other sectors, spending on defence military programmes increased by US$48 billion, or 6%, over the year to US$917 billion.
Taken together, a Treasury official estimates the US deficit-to-GDP ratio is around 6.2%, up from 5.8% last year.
This stands in contrast to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's previously stated goal of bringing the deficit down to 3% of GDP, alongside other targets like spurring economic growth of 3%.
The latest budget figures come less than three weeks before US midterm elections, where Trump's Republican party is fighting to retain control of Congress.
Ahead of the crucial vote, both Republicans and Democrats have raised ideas that could widen the budget shortfall further.
Trump recently promised US$5,000 to every American adult if Republicans maintained control of Congress, a plan that would cost over US$1 trillion.
Democrats say they are looking to reverse Medicaid cuts and revive health care tax breaks.

28dfcdfd4e7b0695: BASEL: Novak Djokovic on Friday received a wildcard entry into the Swiss Indoors Basel, setting up his first appearance at the tournament since 2011 as the 24-times Grand Slam champion pursues a place at the ATP Finals and the 103rd title of his career.

The 39-year-old Serbian arrives in Switzerland after a mixed Asian swing, where he captured a record seventh China Open crown before suffering a surprise second-round defeat by Poland's Hubert Hurkacz at the Shanghai Masters, a tournament he has won a record four times.
Djokovic has endured an uneven season by his lofty standards. The former world number one exited the US Open in the first round, his earliest Grand Slam defeat since the 2006 Australian Open.

The decision to add Basel to his schedule comes as something of a surprise after Djokovic said following his early exit in Shanghai that he planned to play only the Paris Masters, scheduled for November 2-8, before the season-ending ATP Finals.

Basel offers Djokovic an opportunity to strengthen his bid for a 17th ATP Finals appearance. He sits 11th in the ATP Live Race to Turin and needs to finish inside the top nine, with world number one Jannik Sinner sidelined for the remainder of 2026 because of a persistent knee injury.
Djokovic will make his fourth appearance in Basel, having lifted the trophy in 2009 by beating Swiss great Roger Federer in the final.
He joins a strong field that includes Canadian Felix Auger-Aliassime and Americans Ben Shelton and Taylor Fritz at the ATP 500 indoor hardcourt event, which runs from Oct 26-Nov 1.
4ae67c51a8bb94f7: NEW YORK: Wall Street ended sharply lower on Friday, with CoreWeave, Broadcom and other AI-related technology stocks under renewed pressure, while a jump in oil prices spooked traders heading into the weekend.
